stories.title: Load policy definitions from a folder or single files
stories.what: Read the administrative template and language files from a chosen folder, or add a single template file, and build the policies and categories people browse.
stories.why: People can only browse and edit policies once their definitions are loaded, and they need to know when something in them could not be used.

terms.name: Definitions
terms.means: The administrative template and language files that describe the policies; not the settings people choose.

criteria.says: Given a folder of template and language files, when the person loads it, then the files are read from that folder and handed on as parsed documents, and the person's own machine is the only place read.

Given a load that finds no problems, when it finishes, then nothing is shown; given problems, then the person sees "Errors were encountered while adding administrative templates to the workspace." with each problem and is asked "Continue trying to use this workspace?" only where a choice is wanted.
Given policies already loaded, when the person adds one template file, then that file alone is added to them, the structures are rebuilt, and a refused file is reported as one failure.

stories.title: Show the category tree and the policies of the chosen area
stories.what: Present the categories of the loaded definitions as a tree with icons, visibility, selection, and a choice of user or computer area.
stories.why: People find a policy by walking the categories, so the tree must show the right ones and keep their place as it changes.

terms.name: Empty category
terms.means: A category with no visible policy and no visible subcategory; not a category that is missing.

criteria.says: Given a category, when its icon is chosen, then it is orphaned first, empty next, and normal otherwise.
Given empty categories are switched off, when a category has no visible policy and no visible subcategory, then it is not visible; when they are switched on, every category is visible.
Given the loaded definitions, when the tree is shown, then only visible categories appear, each with its icon and its visible subcategories below it, sorted.
Given the category shown in the right pane changes, when the tree updates, then its selection follows that category.
Given the tree is rebuilt from newly loaded definitions, when it finishes, then nothing is selected and the information pane shows the empty state.
Given a category is selected in the tree, when the person selects it, then it becomes the current category and any selected policy is cleared.
Given the "Empty Categories" menu, when the person switches empty categories on or off, then the view moves to the nearest visible category.
Given the area choice, when it is "User", then user policies show; "Computer", computer policies; any other choice, both.

Given the list is rebuilt, when the earlier policy is still in the category shown and visible, then it is selected and revealed and the earlier top row is put back if the list still has that many rows; otherwise nothing is selected.

stories.title: Read and write policy files byte for byte
stories.what: Turn the bytes of a policy file into entries and entries back into bytes, with its signature, version, text and number encodings, ordering and duplicate handling.
stories.why: Policy files are what Windows reads, so a file saved here must be read back exactly and a bad file must be refused with a clear message.

terms.name: Policy file
terms.means: A saved file of policy settings for one machine or user; not the definitions that describe the policies.

criteria.says: Given text in a policy file, when it is read, then it stops at its first empty character, and a multiple-string value ends at its first empty string.

Given a stored value, when it is read back, then it is text for text and expandable text, a 32-bit or 64-bit number for numbers, a list of strings for multiple strings, and raw bytes for every other type.
Given a file whose format version is not 1, when it is read, then it is refused with 'Unknown (newer) version of POL format'.
Given a file that does not start with the 'PReg' signature, when it is read, then it is refused with 'Missing PReg signature'.
Given an extra empty character after a value name, when the file is read, then it is skipped, as Microsoft's documentation allows.
Given entries, when the file is saved, then they are written in alphabetical order so a key-clearing marker comes before the values it clears.
Given a multiple-string value, when it is saved, then each string is followed by an empty character and one more empty character closes the list.
Given a 64-bit number, when it is saved, then it is 8 bytes, lowest byte first.
Given a 32-bit number, when it is saved, then it is 4 bytes, lowest byte first.
Given text, when it is saved, then it is written in two-byte characters followed by a closing empty character.
Given a value, when it is saved, then text, expandable text, 32-bit and 64-bit numbers and multiple strings are stored by their stated type and every other type as raw bytes with that type.
Given the same key and value name twice in a file, when it is read, then the later entry wins, names match without regard to letter case, and the first spelling seen is kept for saving.

stories.title: Hold a policy file's settings in memory and answer questions about them
stories.what: Keep the entries of one policy file and answer whether a value is present, read it, set it, forget it, mark it for deletion or clear a key.
stories.why: Applying policies and checking what a file says depend on these answers being exact, including what is marked for deletion.

terms.name: Marked for deletion
terms.means: A value the file says should be removed on the machine; not a value that is merely absent.

criteria.says: Given a policy file, when a value is checked, then it counts as marked for deletion when a deletion marker, a clear-all marker or a delete-values list names it, regardless of case, and a later-sorting value of that name cancels the deletion.
Given a key, when its values are listed, then marker entries are left out unless the caller asks for them.
Given a value that is absent or marked for deletion, when it is read, then nothing is given.
Given a value, when its presence is asked, then it counts as present only if it is stored and not marked for deletion.
Given an expected deletion marker, number or text, when presence is tested, then it is present if marked, an equal whole number, or equal text; a value of the wrong kind is not present.
Given a value, when it is marked for deletion, then anything held under that name is dropped and a marker holding 32 is added unless already marked or its key is cleared.
Given a value, when it is set, then it replaces any value under that name and a deletion marker for the name is kept.
Given a value, when it is forgotten, then both the value and its marker are removed so the policy says nothing about it.
Given a key, when it is cleared, then all values and markers under it are dropped and a single clear-all marker is stored.

stories.title: Read and write the machine's live policy settings
stories.what: Read, write, delete and clear the live policy settings of the machine, check the root names and test whether they can be written.
stories.why: People apply policies straight to the machine, so this source must behave as the machine's own settings do.

terms.name: Live settings
terms.means: The policy settings currently in force on the machine; not a saved policy file.

criteria.says: Given the machine's settings are reached from the person's own machine, when they are read or changed, then the service does so on that machine only and the web app never does.
Given the live settings, when a value is checked for deletion, then it is never reported as marked for deletion.

Given a key and a value name, when presence is asked, then it is present when the key exists and, unless the name is empty, the key lists that name regardless of case; an empty name means the key itself.
Given a missing key, when a value is read, then nothing is given; signed numbers come back as the unsigned numbers policies use and environment variables in text are not expanded.
Given an unsigned 32-bit or 64-bit number, when it is saved, then it is stored as the signed number with the same bits and the key is created if missing.
Given a key that does not exist, when a value is deleted, then nothing happens and no error is shown.
Given a value, when it is forgotten, then it is deleted, since a pending deletion cannot be remembered.
Given a key, when it is cleared, then every value in it is deleted but the key and its subkeys stay; forgetting a key's clearance does nothing.
Given a settings source, when a test value cannot be written under Software\Policies and removed again, then the source is read-only.

Given a source path, when it does not start with HKCU, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, HKU, HKEY_USERS, HKLM or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE in any case, then it is refused with "The root key is not valid."; otherwise the path is opened and created if missing.

stories.title: Open another user's stored settings file as a source
stories.what: Load a user's stored settings file into the machine under a temporary name and unload it when the source is released.
stories.why: People can edit the policies of a user who is not signed in, and the machine must be left as it was.

terms.name: User hive
terms.means: A user's stored settings file; not the live settings of the signed-in user.

criteria.says: Given a user's stored settings file, when it is used as a source, then it is loaded under a fresh temporary name after the backup and restore rights are switched on, by the service on the person's machine.
Given the file cannot be opened after loading, when the source is used, then it silently becomes an empty read-only scratch source.
Given a source is closed, when it is a mounted user hive, then it is unloaded and the result tells whether that succeeded; every other kind of source closes successfully.

stories.title: Export settings to a registry text file
stories.what: Collect the settings destined for an exported registry text file, limited to a branch, and refuse every read or check.
stories.why: People can save policies as a registry text file to share or import, and must be told plainly when a file cannot be read back.

terms.name: Registry export file
terms.means: A registry text file made to import settings elsewhere; not a policy file.

criteria.says: Given a registry export file, when a value is checked for deletion, then the request fails with 'not implemented'.
Given a registry export file, when a value is read, then the request fails with 'not implemented'.
Given a registry export file, when a key's values are listed, then the request fails with 'not implemented'.
Given a registry export file, when presence is asked, then the request fails with 'not implemented'.
Given a registry export file, when a value is forgotten, then the request fails with 'not implemented'.
Given a value is saved, when a branch is set and its key lies outside it, then it is ignored; with no branch every key is accepted, and any value under that name is replaced.
Given a value is deleted, when a branch is set and the key lies outside it or the key is already marked for removal, then it is ignored; otherwise the value is recorded as deleted.
Given a key is cleared, when a branch is set and it lies outside, then it is ignored; otherwise its earlier entries are replaced by a key-removal entry.

open: Applying a newer policy file over an older one to a registry export file fails for any dropped value under a policy branch; should the target keep this failure or support it?
